source: Abel et al. (2019) Sleep reduces the testing effect, but not after corrective feedback and prolonged retention interval - Exp 1a
finding: Replicates Baeuml, Holterman and Abel (2014). Across 12 h, sleep helps restudied items but not retrieval-practised items (no feedback). So the testing effect (less forgetting after retrieval) shows after 12 h awake, not after 12 h asleep. This is the opposite of retrieval and sleep adding up.
numbers: Exp 1a (36 per delay cell, 3 delays, one practice cycle): sleep vs wake recall, restudy 70.6% vs 48.8% (d=0.78); retrieval with feedback 65.1% vs 45.8% (d=0.75); retrieval without feedback 54.6% vs 51.2% (t<1). Test x delay interaction wake: F(1,70)=29.81, np2=.30; sleep: F=1.73, p=.193.
limits: Paired associates only. Direct testing effect absent after 12 h in Exp 1a because restudy led by about 20 points at short delay.
agent_relevance: Retrieval and sleep overlap, so they are not additive. An agent should not assume that a retrieval pass plus an offline consolidation pass gives double benefit.

source: Abel et al. (2019) Sleep reduces the testing effect, but not after corrective feedback and prolonged retention interval - Exp 1b
finding: Three practice cycles instead of one gave the same pattern. Practice level does not change the sleep x retrieval interaction.
numbers: Exp 1b: sleep vs wake restudy 85.8% vs 73.6% (d=0.51); retrieval with feedback 88.9% vs 75.4% (d=0.65); retrieval without feedback 73.3% vs 70.5% (t<1). Short-delay: restudy 92.7%, retrieval with feedback 93.4%, retrieval without 75.4%. Wake test x delay F(1,70)=9.65, np2=.12; sleep F<1.
limits: Ceiling effects at short delay (above 90%).
agent_relevance: Corrective feedback after a failed retrieval matters: without it, unretrieved items are lost. For an agent, a retrieval step needs a feedback or verify step.

source: Abel et al. (2019) Sleep reduces the testing effect, but not after corrective feedback and prolonged retention interval - Exp 2a/2b
finding: The sleep modulation is short-lived. At 24 h and 7 days there was no lasting sleep benefit on either restudy or retrieval items, and the usual testing effect (less forgetting) was present whether sleep or wake followed encoding.
numbers: Exp 2a (N=160, n=32 per cell, 5 delays): 12-h wake test x delay F(1,62)=15.08, np2=.20; sleep F=1.13, p=.292. 7-day: test x delay F(1,62)>=17.76, np2=.22 in both. 7-day recall restudy 33.8% vs retrieval 37.5%. Exp 2b N=128: same at 24 h and 7 d.
limits: Finnish-German vocabulary and unrelated word pairs. The authors say the result surprised them because they predicted lasting sleep benefits.
agent_relevance: Any claimed retrieval-speeds-consolidation effect must be checked at delays of days; short-delay gains can vanish.

source: Liu, Ranganath and O'Reilly (2024) A complementary learning systems model of how sleep moderates retrieval practice effects. Psychon Bull Rev 31:2022-2035
finding: Summarises Liu and Ranganath (2021): no global effect of sleep on retention and no general change in retrieval-practice effects on untested items. Only one result depended on sleep: retrieval practice hurt temporally far, semantically related pairmates when people stayed awake, but helped them after sleep. A hippocampus-cortex model (TEACH) reproduces this.
numbers: Model 3-way interaction (proximity x relatedness x sleep): F(1,38)=20.21, p<.001, np2=.35. Model far+related: sleep facilitation t(19)=4.25, d=0.95; wake impairment t(19)=3.13, d=0.70. Rival sleep rules fail: Sleep-AddRP (sleep = extra retrieval) gives impairment d=0.67 not facilitation; Sleep-PriWeak impairment d=1.05; Sleep-All null t(19)=.97.
quote: Retrieval practice impaired retention of temporally far, semantically related pairs if subjects were unable to sleep
limits: Computational fit to one behavioural dataset, 20 simulated subjects per cell. Authors note behavioural sleep effects are inconsistent across paradigms.
agent_relevance: Sleep replay is not the same as retrieval. Offline consolidation (re-reading stored notes, summarising) may do a different job from online retrieval. Keep them as separate operators.

source: Liu and Ranganath (2021) Psychon Bull Rev 28(6):2035-2044, as reported in Liu et al. (2024)
finding: Retrieval practice always helps temporally close untested pairmates (retrieval-induced facilitation) and always hurts far, unrelated ones (retrieval-induced forgetting). Sleep flips only the far-and-related case from harm to help: it lets people integrate across separate episodes.
numbers: Human effect sizes not in the 2024 text I read; numbers above are from the model fit.
limits: Second-hand: numbers for the 2021 human data not read.
agent_relevance: Retrieval may damage related but unretrieved memories unless a later integration step follows. Matters for agent memory write and update policies.

source: Parks, Mohawk, Werner and Kiley (2022) The time window of reconsolidation: A replication. Psychon Bull Rev
finding: Direct replication of Hupbach et al. (2007) reminder-then-new-learning updating. The 3-day result replicated (reminder group had more List-2 intrusions). The 2-day (no time window) null replicated. But the no-reminder group also showed more intrusions than control, which Hupbach did not find.
numbers: N=132 planned (22 per cell; 66 per experiment). Exp 1 intrusions: reminder > no-reminder t(42)=3.34, d=1.01, BF10=39.3; no-reminder > control t(42)=3.98, d=1.20, BF10=187.5. Exp 2 (immediate test) reminder vs no-reminder null. Power from Scully meta-analysis mean d=1.03. List-1 recall: no-reminder beat reminder t(42)=-2.04, d=-.62, BF10=1.54 (anecdotal).
limits: Object lists, one lab, UNLV students. Some no-reminder testing moved to another building (COVID). Time dependence can also be explained by context accounts.
agent_relevance: Reminding an old trace and then adding new content makes new content leak into the old memory. In an agent, retrieving a note and then writing new facts in the same context risks cross-contamination.

source: Hupbach, Gomez, Hardt and Nadel (2007) Learning & Memory 14:47-53, as described in Parks et al. (2022)
finding: Founding human behavioural reconsolidation study: a reminder of Day-1 learning before learning List 2 gave more List-2 intrusions into List-1 recall two days later. No effect when tested immediately.
numbers: Learned to 85% criterion (17 of 20 objects). Effect sizes not reported in the original (per Parks et al.).
limits: Second-hand description only.
agent_relevance: Origin of the retrieval-opens-a-labile-window idea, often confused with retrieval-as-consolidation.

source: Scully, Napper and Hupbach (2017) Does reactivation trigger episodic memory change? A meta-analysis. Neurosci Biobehav Rev
finding: Meta-analysis finds reactivation makes episodic memory open to physiological and behavioural interference. New learning after reactivation reliably raises intrusions from the new material into the old memory. Stronger for remote memories and narrative material.
numbers: Mean d=1.03 over eight List-2 intrusion effect sizes (as quoted by Parks et al. 2022).
limits: Abstract only via Europe PMC; intrusion can also be explained by context or retroactive interference.
agent_relevance: Intrusion (leakage) is the reliable effect, not erasure.

source: Hardwicke, Taqi and Shanks (2016) Postretrieval new learning does not reliably induce human memory updating via reconsolidation. PNAS 113:5206-5211
finding: Four direct and three conceptual replications of Walker et al. (2003) motor-sequence reconsolidation found no reconsolidation effect. In the declarative tasks, retrieval appeared to help keep old sequence knowledge instead of making it vulnerable.
numbers: Direct replications n=64 total (4 attempts); conceptual n=48 (3 attempts).
limits: Read abstract and significance statement via NCBI only.
agent_relevance: Retrieval protected old content in this task. Another sign the labile-window story is fragile.

source: Levy, Mika, Radzyminski, Ben-Zvi and Tibon (2018) Behavioral reconsolidation interference with episodic memory within-subjects is elusive. NeuroImage
finding: Three within-subject experiments over three days (reminder plus retroactive interference, recognition test without intrusions) found no effect on accuracy, response times, recollection or confidence. Bayesian tests supported the null.
numbers: Three experiments, N=40 each analysed (5 excluded in Exp 1). 200 object pictures. Bayes factors reported in the paper range from about 4 to 14.
limits: Recognition of picture exemplars; authors suggest boundary conditions (intrusion-free measure, within-subject design).
agent_relevance: The strongest published effect evidence rests on between-subject intrusion counts. Treat reconsolidation-style update-by-retrieval claims as weak.

source: Craig, Dewar and colleagues (2021) A study on episodic memory reconsolidation that tells us more about consolidation. Learn Mem 28(2)
finding: Tried to show that quiet rest after retrieval supports reconsolidation of object-location memory. Could not probe it, but found a delayed effect of rest on consolidation of non-retrieved memory.
numbers: N=60 (30 rest, 30 filler); 60 object-location items, 30 retrieved in the first test; 10-min delays.
quote: We failed to probe the effect of quiescence on reconsolidation
limits: Authors state they failed to probe the reconsolidation question. Small sample, one task.
agent_relevance: Rest-state consolidation also acts after a task phase. Weak support for adding idle consolidation steps.

source: Antony, Ferreira, Norman and Wimber (2017) Retrieval as a fast route to memory consolidation. Trends Cogn Sci 21:573-576
finding: Core hypothesis: retrieval is a rapid consolidation event that integrates a memory with neocortical knowledge and differentiates it from competitors, making it less hippocampus-dependent. Predicts vmPFC up and hippocampus down for retrieved vs restudied items. Predicts that benefits shrink for novel materials with no neocortical schema (nonsense drawings or syllables).
numbers: No new data. Box 1 lists predictions: representational differentiation, competitor weakening, more insight and inference after retrieval than restudy, reduced context dependence.
quote: retrieval acts as a rapid consolidation event
limits: Perspective article, 4 pages. Several predictions later got mixed support (Abel 2019, Ferreira and Wimber 2023, Ashton 2022).
agent_relevance: Supports a design where retrieval passes link new items to existing knowledge. The schema-dependence prediction is directly testable and partly confirmed.

source: Ye, Shi, Li, Chen and Xue (2020) Retrieval practice facilitates memory updating by enhancing and differentiating medial prefrontal cortex representations. eLife 9:e57023
finding: fMRI A-B/A-C updating over three days. Retrieval practice of the new pairing, compared with restudy, strengthened new memory and cut old-memory intrusions without suppressing the old memory. mPFC target evidence was stronger. This supports the integration and differentiation account.
numbers: Exp 1 n=19 fMRI. Exp 2 n=46: A-C correct recall higher under retrieval, t(45)=3.93, d=0.57; fewer competitor intrusions t(45)=-2.75, p=.008, d=0.36. A-B memory 55.9% correct, no update-method effect (p=.19).
limits: Small fMRI sample; a reviewer flagged a 3-class classifier confound. Word-picture pairs.
agent_relevance: Retrieval-based update is a way to replace a stale fact without erasing the old one. Useful design for agent memory revision.

source: Ferreira and Wimber (2023) The testing effect for visual materials depends on preexisting knowledge. J Exp Psychol Learn Mem Cogn 49:1557-1571
finding: Tests the schema-dependence prediction. Meaningless squiggles never showed a testing benefit (two experiments, immediate and 1-week). Meaningful object images did, mainly after 1 week and with a recollection-focused test. Immediately, restudy was better.
numbers: Four experiments; Exp 1B had 48 participants (24 retrieval, 24 restudy); delays immediate vs 1 week. No testing benefit for squiggles in 1A or 1B; for meaningful objects, restudy better immediately, retrieval better after delay (strongest in Exp 2B, recognition with remember/know).
quote: Abstract shapes never showed a significant testing benefit
limits: Between-subject practice groups; visual recognition, not text. The authors say Exp 1B evidence is not strong for or against any theory.
agent_relevance: Retrieval helps most when the item connects to prior knowledge. For an agent, retrieval over notes should tie new facts to existing structure; random facts gain less.

source: Ashton, Staresina and Cairney (2022) Sleep bolsters schematically incongruent memories. PLoS ONE 17:e0269439
finding: Pre-registered online test of schema and rehearsal on overnight consolidation. Sleep amplified consolidation for restudied more than retrieval-practised items, only when sleep came soon after learning. Schema-congruent pairs were remembered better overall, but sleep helped incongruent pairs more. This runs against schema-consistent information consolidating faster.
numbers: Final N=60 after 2 napping exclusions; noun-colour pairs; 12 h sleep or wake, tests at 12 h and 24 h.
quote: These findings challenge the notion that schema-conformant memories are preferentially strengthened
limits: Read abstract and design only. Online data, one material type.
agent_relevance: The schema-consistent-integrates-faster claim is not safe. Do not build an agent rule that prioritises schema-fit facts for consolidation.

source: Gupta, Pan and Rickard (2021) Prior episodic learning and the efficacy of retrieval practice. Mem Cogn
finding: Across three experiments the testing advantage over restudy did not depend on how well items were first studied (1, 4 or 8 study repetitions). This fits a dual-memory model and speaks against a prior-learning moderator.
numbers: Exp 1 N=95 (49 at 1x, 46 at 4x), 80 pairs; training test accuracy .217 vs .55, d=0.46. Exp 2 N=129 analysed (4x vs 8x), training .463 vs .600, d=0.38. Exp 3 N=51 within-subject. Bayes factor for the key interaction favours null (BF01=4.52).
limits: Episodic prior learning, not semantic schema. Word pairs, final tests at 1 to 2 days.
agent_relevance: Strength of first encoding does not change the gain from a retrieval pass, so retrieval passes are broadly worth it for items already stored.

source: Rowland (2014) The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: a meta-analytic review of the testing effect. Psychol Bull 140:1432-1463
finding: Meta-analysis: recall tests give larger testing benefits than recognition tests (effort matters). Limited support for semantic elaboration accounts; episodic and contextual accounts and the bifurcation model are favoured.
numbers: Exact g not read in this session.
limits: Abstract only. Does not test consolidation directly.
agent_relevance: Effortful free recall beats recognition: ask the agent to generate, not merely confirm.

source: Retrieval training vs sleep EEG phase similarity study (2026) Imaging Neuroscience, doi:10.1162/IMAG.a.1321
finding: First direct comparison of retrieval training and sleep (plus restudy and wake) on representational change. Only retrieval training produced extra merging of similar-object EEG patterns (alpha band, parieto-occipital), and retrieval training lowered discrimination of similar lures. Sleep and retrieval give different transformations over equal time.
numbers: N=30 (27 F), four 120-min interventions within subject (retrieval, restudy, sleep, wake). Merging predicted better lure discrimination across people despite worse average discrimination.
quote: sleep and retrieval training induce different memory transformations across equivalent timescales
limits: Small sample, object-word pairs, EEG phase measure; I read the abstract and methods text only; first author not extracted.
agent_relevance: Retrieval produces gist extraction with a cost to fine detail. An agent should keep verbatim source text next to retrieved-and-summarised notes.

source: An, Acharya, Liu and Hashmi (2025) Enhancing student learning with LLM-generated retrieval practice questions. arXiv:2507.05629
finding: Quasi-experiment: LLM-written multiple-choice retrieval practice in lectures raised quiz accuracy the following week. Same students, two different weeks, no randomisation.
numbers: Quiz 1 (LLM retrieval) mean .89, median .95, n=31; Quiz 2 (no retrieval) mean .73, median .75, n=27. Mann-Whitney U=703, Z=4.46, p<.0001, rank-biserial r=0.586. About 60 students, 2 courses, weeks 6-9.
limits: Confounded by week, topic and quiz difficulty; not randomised; anonymous quizzes treated as independent groups; questions needed human checks (duplicated options, hallucination).
agent_relevance: Shows LLM tools can deliver retrieval practice to humans. It does not test whether an LLM itself consolidates by retrieval.

source: Panthi, Yeamin, Luo and Abdelfattah (2026) Memory consolidation flattens the temporal shape of user facts (LAPSE). arXiv:2609.36457
finding: Agent memory systems that rewrite chats into short notes lose aspect: 'I am working at X' becomes 'The user works at X'. This one-way loss held in all 11 models and in mem0, Graphiti and Letta. Readers then act on the flattened note more.
numbers: Writers flattened progressive but kept simple-present in 210 of 381 pairs, never the reverse. Reader GLM-5.2 acted without asking on 64% of 'works' notes vs 40% of 'is working' notes; smaller gap for Gemini 3 Flash, reversed for one reader, none for others. Keeping the user's words restored the difference.
limits: Parts exploratory; effect varies by reader model.
agent_relevance: Engineering consolidation is lossy for uncertainty cues. Keep raw wording as evidence beside any compressed note.

source: Kwon (2026) Manufactured confidence: how memory consolidation turns hearsay into confident facts. arXiv:2606.29279
finding: Memory rewriting in LLM agents turns a hedged remark into a flat dated fact that agents then obey. The model responds to phrasing confidence, not source. Passive unverified tags are ignored; do-not-trust prompts escalate even correct memory. One redundant source restores correct decisions.
numbers: Cascade of confident-wrong output on all five models tested. No sample counts in the abstract.
limits: Constructed agent settings, independent researcher, preprint.
agent_relevance: Consolidation step must keep hedges. Require two independent notes before an action-relevant fact is trusted.

source: Xie (2026) Learning to forget: sleep-inspired memory consolidation for proactive interference in LLMs (SleepGate). arXiv:2603.14517
finding: A learned sleep cycle on the KV cache (tag conflicts, forget, merge) restored retrieval of the newest value under proactive interference in a tiny synthetic setting. Baselines stayed near chance.
numbers: 793K-parameter 4-layer transformer, synthetic key-value streams, N=200 episodes per depth. SleepGate 99.0-99.5% accuracy at n=2-5 prior updates, 97.0% at n=10; best baseline (StreamingLLM) 18.0% at n=2 and 10.0% at n=5. Accuracy fell to 16.5% at n=30 (stale retrieval 62%). Depth-1 accuracy 82.5%.
limits: Proof of concept only; synthetic; not a pre-trained LLM; no retrieval-practice variable.
agent_relevance: Supersession-aware forgetting is cheap to try as a notes policy: tag older values as superseded.

source: Kyrkewood (2026) The Sleeping Agent: what gist-based context compression loses and why. arXiv:2608.11775
finding: Sleep-inspired salience-weighted gist compression beats truncation and sliding window on LoCoMo but fails on temporal questions because dates are dropped. Protecting temporal anchors fixes most of it.
numbers: LoCoMo, 10 conversations, 1,501 questions per condition. SWC-Temporal accuracy 0.468, +0.298 over truncation, +0.231 over sliding window. Temporal category: SWC-Temporal minus SWC-Full +0.314 [0.254, 0.375], n=315; SWC-Full temporal accuracy 0.156. Only 3.05% of temporal expressions survive generic gist vs 62.39% with temporal protection. LLM judge (Haiku) 95% agreement with 60 human labels.
limits: Independent preprint; judge is an LLM; compression is not retrieval practice.
agent_relevance: Gist consolidation costs specific detail. Mirrors the human result that retrieval training extracts gist and loses lure discrimination.

source: Gap check: arXiv searches (this session) for LLM retrieval practice, testing effect, retrieval-induced forgetting, reconsolidation
finding: Searches combining retrieval practice, testing effect, retrieval-induced forgetting or reconsolidation with language models found only human-education studies (An 2025) and engineering memory-consolidation papers. No controlled LLM test of the retrieval-as-consolidation claim was found.
numbers: About eleven arXiv queries run; no relevant hits for RIF or reconsolidation in LLMs.
limits: Absence of evidence in a limited search (arXiv only; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate limited).
agent_relevance: Open gap: an agent test could compare answer-from-memory-then-check against reread on a later notes-based task.

source: Baeuml, Holterman and Abel (2014) Sleep benefits restudy more than retrieval practice (original finding, as described in Abel et al. 2019)
finding: Original 12-h study: sleep right after encoding helped restudied items but not retrieval-practised items, which reduced or removed the testing effect after sleep. Explained by a bifurcation model in which sleep strengthens all items about equally, so strong retrieved items gain little.
numbers: Numbers not in the text I read; Abel et al. 2019 reproduced the pattern in Exp 1a, 1b and 2a (see b01-b03).
limits: Second-hand description. The original found a direct testing effect after wake; Abel et al. did not in Exp 1a because restudy led by about 20 points at short delay.
agent_relevance: Rival account to retrieval-as-consolidation: retrieval and sleep strengthen the same trace, so they substitute, not stack.
